EO 6205-B (1933-07-15) hearing procedure; EO 6407, 6424, 6463, 6476 cotton-textile stay orders; SHARED_ANALYSIS.md section on denials of exemption tested on the merits; owner ruling 2026-10-28
reasoning: The shared analysis's section on denials of exemption was tested on the merits and holds. Under EO 6205-B (July 15, 1933, held text) an approved code is 'in full force and effect on the effective date as stated in the code'; a timely applicant receives a hearing and determination 'prior to incurring any liability to enforcement of the code'. The denial therefore does one thing on its date: it disposes of the application and ends the pre-determination protection. The applicants' continuing duty to comply afterwards comes from the approving order through section 3(b), (c) and (f), not from the denial: had the approval been cancelled earlier the denial would have had no work to do, and a later exemption would have been a new grant, not a revocation of the denial. The owner ruling of 2026-10-28 (rule 1) requires a one-time command used on its date to be recorded as exhausted by performance, and rule 3 requires a reason before a later general rule supplies an end; the repeal had nothing of the denial left to extinguish. The claim considers this reading and rejects it by attributing the code's continuing force to the denial, which conflates the two orders. Its judgment_reason and savings text are also the approval template: they call this denial 'this approval' and say the judgment 'did not cancel or withdraw this approval', which misdescribes the instrument. Text, identity (APP heading, register, WPA 'Application of the Crystal Springs Bleachery for exemptions ... denied. I NRA Codes 726.') and quotes all check out; the defects are the legal characterization, the missing exception clause, and the template mislabeling. The claim's description of EO 6407 as only 'setting' the stay's termination also omits that EO 6407 itself denied the tire-yarn exemption application (later reopened by EO 6463 and denied again by EO 6476); this is minor. reasoning: The shared analysis's section on denials of exemption was tested on the merits and holds. Under EO 6205-B (July 15, 1933, held text) an approved code is 'in full force and effect on the effective date as stated in the code'; a timely applicant receives a hearing and determination 'prior to incurring any liability to enforcement of the code'. The denial therefore does one thing on its date: it disposes of the application and ends the pre-determination protection. The applicants' continuing duty to comply afterwards comes from the approving order through section 3(b), (c) and (f), not from the denial: had the approval been cancelled earlier the denial would have had no work to do, and a later exemption would have been a new grant, not a revocation of the denial. The owner ruling of 2026-10-28 (rule 1) requires a one-time command used on its date to be recorded as exhausted by performance, and rule 3 requires a reason before a later general rule supplies an end; the repeal had nothing of the denial left to extinguish. The claim considers this reading and rejects it by attributing the code's continuing force to the denial, which conflates the two orders. Its judgment_reason and savings text are also the approval template: they call this denial 'this approval' and say the judgment 'did not cancel or withdraw this approval', which misdescribes the instrument. II NRA Codes 696.') and quotes check out, and the later Lumber code orders the claim cites (EO 6255, 6323, 6487, 6654) are correctly dated and are not ends; the defect is the legal characterization of the denial and the template mislabeling.
